reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Bolognia Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin and subcutis, presenting as firm white or yellow papules, nodules or plaques that may ulcerate and extrude chalky, toothpaste-like material
Classified into four main types: dystrophic (much the commonest), metastatic, idiopathic and iatrogenic, with calciphylaxis considered a distinct and dangerous vascular variant

Dystrophic calcinosis occurs in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium and phosphate, classically complicating connective tissue disease such as juvenile dermatomyositis and systemic sclerosis (the C of CREST)
Metastatic calcinosis reflects a deranged calcium-phosphate product, seen in chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D, sarcoidosis and milk-alkali syndrome

Idiopathic forms include idiopathic scrotal calcinosis, subepidermal calcified nodules and tumoral calcinosis, while iatrogenic disease follows extravasation of calcium- or phosphate-containing infusions
Investigation is directed at the calcium-phosphate axis and any underlying connective tissue disease, with radiographs delineating the extent and distribution of deposits

Treatment is difficult and evidence is limited; options include correcting metabolic drivers, medical therapies such as sodium thiosulfate, warfarin, bisphosphonates, minocycline and diltiazem, and surgical excision of symptomatic deposits
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous calcinosis results from precipitation of calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) or amorphous calcium salts within the dermis or subcutaneous tissue. In dystrophic disease, local tissue injury, inflammation and mitochondrial calcium overload in damaged cells provide a nidus for mineralisation despite normal circulating calcium and phosphate; release of phosphate-binding proteins and denatured collagen and elastin favour crystal nucleation. In metastatic disease, a raised calcium-phosphate product drives deposition in otherwise normal tissue, particularly where local pH or tissue conditions promote precipitation. Idiopathic and iatrogenic forms reflect, respectively, unexplained local deposition and direct introduction of calcium salts, while calciphylaxis involves medial calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels causing ischaemic necrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Calciphylaxis (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy) when painful ischaemic ulceration predominates
Cutaneous ossification (osteoma cutis) and osteoma cutis of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy
Gouty tophi and other crystal deposition
Subcutaneous nodules of rheumatoid disease or rheumatic fever
Epidermoid or pilar cysts and other adnexal tumours
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and alkaline phosphatase to define the metabolic type
Renal function tests to identify chronic kidney disease
Plain radiography (and where needed CT) to map the distribution and burden of calcification
Skin biopsy with von Kossa or alizarin red staining to confirm calcium deposition
Autoimmune serology including antinuclear and myositis-specific antibodies when connective tissue disease is suspected
Screening for sarcoidosis or occult malignancy where metastatic calcification is unexplained
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful retiform ulceration suggesting calciphylaxis
Secondary infection or systemic sepsis arising from ulcerated deposits
Widespread metastatic calcification indicating severe metabolic derangement
Functional loss from periarticular deposits causing contracture or nerve compression
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the type and underlying cause: idiopathic and iatrogenic deposits may resolve or remain stable, whereas dystrophic calcinosis of connective tissue disease is often chronic, recurrent and resistant to therapy. Metastatic calcinosis improves when the calcium-phosphate disturbance is corrected, while calciphylaxis carries high morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming normal serum calcium excludes significant disease, when most cutaneous calcinosis is dystrophic with a normal calcium-phosphate axis
Overlooking an underlying connective tissue disease, particularly juvenile dermatomyositis or systemic sclerosis
Missing calciphylaxis, which requires urgent recognition and differs fundamentally in management and prognosis
Aggressive surgery precipitating poor wound healing, recurrence at operative sites and new dystrophic deposits
Failing to review medications and infusions as an iatrogenic source of calcium loading
management: Correct the underlying calcium-phosphate disturbance in metastatic disease using phosphate binders, treatment of hyperparathyroidism and withdrawal of excess vitamin D
Treat the underlying connective tissue disease with immunosuppression in dystrophic calcinosis of dermatomyositis or systemic sclerosis
Trial of medical therapies such as the calcium-channel blocker diltiazem, sodium thiosulfate, bisphosphonates or colchicine for symptomatic deposits
Surgical excision of painful, ulcerating or functionally limiting calcified deposits
Urgent management of calciphylaxis with sodium thiosulfate, wound care and correction of mineral metabolism
Wound care and treatment of secondary infection when deposits ulcerate and extrude chalky material
Refer to dermatology with rheumatology or nephrology input according to the underlying cause
